Chemical Engineering
The department of chemical engineering develops solutions for societal problems, leveraging our broad expertise in chemical engineering, chemistry, physics and materials science. We harness our scientific curiosity to define emerging fundamental questions and educate future leaders in the field of chemical engineering.
The scientific staff of the department is formed by independent Principle Investigators.The PIs are clustered in sections which provide a social structure, ensure safety, maintain the infrastructure and constitute the disciplinary basis of the research.

Daiqi Lin received the ‘Young Talent Research Grant’
On Wednesday, May 20, 2026, Daiqi Lin, PhD candidate at Department of Chemical Engineering, Kenjeres Lab, received the ‘Young Talent Research Grant’ (in value of 5kEuro) for his project proposal entitled: “AortaFlowGPT: a large language model for CFD simulation on the blood flow of aortic aneurysm” from the Aneurysm-NL research network. Daiqi Lin: "I feel really honored to be awarded the 'Young Talent Research Grant' from Aneurysm-NL. My project focuses on developing a user-friendly CFD tool for simulating blood flow in aortic aneurysms and related diseases. The received funding will be used to purchase the computational resources, such as a local workstation with advanced GPUs, which will enable integrating the large language model (LLM) into CFD workflow. The funding will also be used for conferences or communication between universities and hospitals, which can promote the clinical application of CFD and improve the impact of Aneurysm-NL community." Photo: Daiqi Lin and Hanneke Takenberg, Professor of Clinical Decision Making in Cardio-Thoracic Interventions, Erasmus University Medical Center, Rotterdam
Letizia Lanza and Margareth Baidun both won poster awards at the Operando VIII Conference
On May 10-14, the Operando VIII Conference was held in Asilomar, California. Two members from our department received awards: Letizia Lanza from the Urakawa Group won second in the poster pitch competition, and third for her poster presentation. Margareth Baidun from the Pidko Group won first place for her poster presentation. Letizia Lanza Margareth Baidun Can you explain what the poster and the pitch were about? Letizia Lanza: "My PhD focuses on new dual functional materials for integrated CO 2 capture and conversion, a strategy to intensify the closure of the carbon cycle. The goal of this project was to develop a material able to carry out the process at low temperatures. In my poster I showed, for this material, the synthesis, catalytic activity and preliminary insights into the active species involved in the reaction using operando diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS). During the conference we also had the chance to pitch our poster. They allocated for each presenter 3 minutes and, with the aid of two slides, I briefly presented the concept of my poster. In the pitch, I gave emphasis to the DRIFTS results and the insights I got with them, as it was the central topic of the conference." Margareth Baidun: “My PhD focuses on the challenge of modeling real catalytic systems in a way that is both realistic and interpretable. Since this was a conference about operando spectroscopy, my goal was to highlight the operando part of my research. Computational chemistry often relies on simplified assumptions, overlooking important aspect that arise during the reaction. In my work, I explicitly include reaction conditions in my simulations to identify which catalyst structures are actually accessible and relevant during catalysis. The goal is to develop models that are realistic enough to capture the important chemistry, while still being simple enough to provide insight into how these catalysts work.” What made your poster and pitch stand out? Letizia Lanza: "Concerning the poster design, I used bright, high contrast colors, big and clear images, with good spacing among the different sections. Moreover, I used the layout not to only show results, but to tell the story of my material and my research. So I selected a limited number of experiments, and conveyed one clear and focused message. The rest was discussed orally with the other researchers during the poster session. Also for the pitch I focused only on one interesting result, regarding operando DRIFTS. I reversed the “usual order”, starting directly with the conclusion of my work rather than giving a context or introduction to the topic. I also used animations and images throughout the presentation to reinforce the message visually, rather than relying only on the spoken explanation." Margareth Baidun: “I think the visual design helped my poster stand out. The title – When Water Turns Poison: Operando Modeling of Ni-Ga Catalyst Deactivation – immediately sparks curiosity. I reinforced that theme through the design, for example by using a slime-inspired font for the word “poison”, a dark background, and a large central visual to attract attention. At the same time, I deliberately kept the content simple. Rather than trying to show everything I have done during my PhD, I focused on explaining the methodology and illustrating it with one clear example.” Why did you approach it that way? Letizia Lanza: “I believe that what first catches people’s attention are bright, high contrast colors, big and clear images. Then, what is remembered is the story one tells rather than individual experimental results. I tried to take both these aspects into account, the first one working on the poster and presentation designs, the second one focusing on conveying one message, with the limited space available. The idea of doing the pitch “reversed”, starting with the operando spectroscopy and the conclusion directly, came from one of my colleagues, who pointed out the fact that the attention to a presentation is higher at the beginning and starting with the main message is the best way to make it catchy. I really liked this advice and decided to implement it in my pitch.” Margareth Baidun: “I believe that, as scientists, it is our job to present our work in an exciting way. Designing posters is one of my favorite parts of communicating science because it allows me to bring some creativity into my research. However, the most important design choice was actually not the visual style, but the decision to keep the poster focused. In my own experience, posters can quickly become overwhelming when they contain too much information. I recently followed a poster design course where one piece of advice really stuck with me: it is better for the audience to remember one message clearly than to forget ten messages presented at once. That idea guided the entire poster design. Judging from the feedback I received, people appreciated that the poster was easy to follow and that the main message came across clearly.” How do you feel about winning these awards, and why? Letizia Lanza: “It is of course rewarding seeing that the great effort I put in doing the poster and the pitch has been rewarded. What I am most happy about, however, is the research itself. I work really hard in my PhD and I became very fond of this project, so what I appreciate the most is seeing that also others liked it and decided to give it recognition.” Margareth Baidun: “Throughout the poster session, I had many engaging discussions with people who were genuinely interested in my research and curious about how computational approaches can contribute to our understanding of catalysts under operando conditions. It was of course very rewarding to receive a prize at the conference. What made it especially meaningful is that I was one of few (if not the only) researchers presenting computational work in an operando-focused community. Seeing that interest, and having my work appreciated by researchers from different backgrounds, makes me even more excited about the direction of my research.”
Bijoy Bera 2026 Educator of the Year for the programs BSc MST & MSc CE
Bijoy Bera has been awarded the ‘Educator of the Year 2026’ prize for the BSc in Molecular Science and Technology and the MSc in Chemical Technology programs. Out of his three consecutive nominations between 2024 and 2026, this is the second time that Bijoy Bera has won this award, the first being in 2024. Students describe him as responsive, committed, helpful, clear, supportive, dedicated, and approachable. He received the award during the TNW Education Afternoon, which took place on 15 June. We asked him a few questions about this: Why is such an award given? “I believe that the award is given to recognize the amazing amount of effort and the great bit of quality that the TU Delft professors are bringing to the table every day. This is also a nice way to figure out to what extent this effort and quality are visible to the people for whom it is done: the students.” Why do you think you were chosen? "I think that my inclusive way of course design, where the needs and wishes of a diverse group of students are accounted for, is accepted well by the students. They like the methodical way I approach education, but also the fact that there is flexibility in the way they are expected to participate. In the end, the fact that I was chosen only tells me that the students are very open about my way of teaching, even if my way of teaching is far from ideal. The credit goes to the students!" What does this distinction mean to you? “It's mainly a humbling experience for me, that inspires me to work harder to collaborate with colleagues and students, in order to keep on contributing to the quality of education in our department/faculty/university.” What do you think of this award? “I think that the nomination shows that our work in the area of education is visible, i.e., if we consider teaching to be a performance then we have an audience. Fellow colleagues being nominated means that we are all in it together, thinking about improving education, and executing that as well. I look forward to being part of this community, where together we can make a difference.” Dr. Bijoy Bera

NGF GroenvermogenNL – Research launched into new production methods for nitrogen-based chemicals
NWO and the National Growth Fund’s GroenvermogenNL programme are making €20.3 million available to make the nitrogen-based chemical industry more sustainable. This will fund the scientific research required for the use of hydrogen and green electrons in the chemical sector. Nitrogen-based chemicals are essential in, among other things, fertilisers, refrigerants, medicines and plastics. The chemical industry is one of the largest users of fossil raw materials and accounts for a significant share of global CO 2 emissions. For example, the production of fertiliser from natural gas accounts for 5% of the Netherlands’ demand for natural gas. Renewable hydrogen could replace this demand. This development will enable the Dutch chemical industry to become more sustainable, whilst also remaining competitive. HyNITROGEN develops energy-efficient, low-carbon technologies that convert renewable electricity into storable chemical energy, helping to combat climate change. The project accelerates flexible routes to green ammonia and other nitrogen products, enabling long-term energy storage and transport and reducing CO 2 emissions from the fossil-based Haber–Bosch value chain. Innovations are scaled up from the lab to early pilots (TRL 2–6) with clear commercialization pathways for fuels, fertilizers, and sustainable chemicals. In addition, nitrogen is recovered from dilute wastewater streams without the use of chemicals, enabling circular use of fertilizers. Funded Project: HyNITROGEN - Green Nitrogen Valorisation Technologies for Sustainable Energy, Fertilisers, and Chemicals Main applicant: Prof. Jimmy Faria Albanese – University of Twente Consortium Partners: Avans University of Applied Sciences, Bosal Netherlands, Casale SA, CATALYZER, CatOlyst B.V., CIRCONICA, DIFFER, Division Q, Ebert Hera, ETB Global, Fluidwell, The Hague University of Applied Sciences, HAN University of Applied Sciences, Hanze University of Applied Sciences Groningen, Hauzer Techno Coating B.V., Hyet NoCarbon, IHI Europe Ltd., Johnson Matthey, MEVALDI B.V., N2 Applied, Nijhuis Water Technology B.V., Nitrovolt, Nobian Industrial Chemicals B.V., Nouryon, ON2Quest, Port of Rotterdam, Radboud University Nijmegen, University of Groningen, Settels Savenije group of companies (STTLS), TNO, TOLSA NETHERLANDS B.V., TOLSA S.A. / Spain, Topsoe R&D, Business Centre Treeport, Delft University of Technology , Eindhoven University of Technology, Umicore AG & Co KG., University of Amsterdam, Leiden University, Maastricht University, University of Twente, Utrecht University, VITALFLUID, Wageningen University & Research. About GroenvermogenNL The National Growth Fund Programme GroenvermogenNL is the investment programme for green assets for the Dutch economy and society. Through this programme, green hydrogen is intended to be the driving force behind the transition from a society and industry based on fossil fuels to a sustainable energy supply. This will enable the Netherlands to build a new industry and an attractive business climate. To make this transition possible, well-trained people and a strong knowledge-sharing structure are essential. The investment programme runs until 2030. Programmes for the National Growth Fund NWO implements thematic programmes for research, knowledge development and innovation funded by the National Growth Fund. The results of these programmes can be applied in innovations and organisations, thereby contributing to the Netherlands’ sustainable earning capacity and broad prosperity. The programmes involve collaboration between parties from across the entire knowledge chain, both public and private.
Carapace Biopolymers, startup founded by Suellen Espindola, has received an NWO Take-Off Phase 2 investment.
Carapace Biopolymers, startup of Suellen Espindola of Chemical Engineering of TU Delft, got a NWO Take Off 2 of 450 k Euros in December. This is a prestigious grant-loan for startups to fast-track innovations. This grant will allow Carapace to get a strong team and to have their laboratory / initial testing facilities. While not widely known, commercial seeds are often treated or coated prior to sowing with synthetic polymer binders and active ingredients for crop protection—such as pesticides and insecticides—as well as plant enhancement. Carapace Biopolymers develops next-generation seed coatings that are bio-based and fully biodegradable by design. These tailored coatings are built on advanced biopolymer processing technologies, are compatible with industry-standard machinery, and enable the delivery of plant biostimulatory compounds alongside the smart integration of biological agents from microbiology and biotechnology. In doing so, the company combines materials science, biotechnology, and agriculture to support a more sustainable industry and foster resilient crops for the future. A recent milestone for the company is the award of an NWO Take-Off Phase 2 investment, which commenced in 2026. This loan is granted to promising academic startups to help translate knowledge and innovation into commercially viable solutions. Following a rigorous selection process -including evaluation by a panel of experts and entrepreneurs-Carapace Biopolymers successfully secured funding for its technology development. The investment will be used to expand the team and establish dedicated laboratory and pilot-scale facilities. Carapace Biopolymers is a spin-off from TU Delft, originating from the ASM/ChemE group - Prof. Stephen Picken, and grounded in fundamental research on biopolymers and sustainable materials. The startup also benefits from support by the environmental biotechnology group on circular biopolymers of microbial origin, with Prof. Mark van Loosdrecht. Founded in 2024, the company was established by Suellen Espíndola (CTO, research and former PhD ASM/ChemE) and Marouschka Blahetek (CEO, background business and finance).
Inspiring children with chemistry experiments during Meet the Professor
Around 25 scientists from TU Delft traded their laboratories and lecture halls for a morning in a primary school classroom. During the sixth Delft edition of Meet the Professor, they gave guest lessons about their own research to children in grades 7 and 8 (final years of primary school). “Every scientist should do this at least once.” Professor Rolf Hut welcomed the professors, assistant professors and associate professors in the morning at the Science Centre, where he spoke about the importance of Meet the Professor. “Our goal is not to attract more children to TU Delft; our goal is to introduce them to science and show them a world they might otherwise never encounter. Today, we are going to inspire them.” More attention for outreach in chemistry This was the main motivation for Tessel Bouwens, who participated in Meet the Professor for the first time. “I’m a chemist, and I’ve noticed that in chemistry there is often little attention for outreach. While the work we do is so important for society and can be explained to children in a really engaging way.” She studies synthetic photosynthesis, which could help address issues such as the global fuel challenge. In the auditorium of the Regenboog School in Tanthof, she explains her research to a group of grade 8 students, who already have a surprisingly strong understanding of photosynthesis. Photosynthesis, photography, and experiments with vinegar The students ask whether there are better ways to capture solar energy than solar panels, whether photosynthesis and photography are related, and what she hopes to achieve with her research. Meanwhile, they experiment with different substances to see what happens when they are combined. Colors appear, and they mix vinegar and baking soda to create a foaming reaction. Tessel is enthusiastic and hopes to participate again next year. “I didn’t expect the children to have explored the topic in such depth already. They asked genuinely interesting questions. I would recommend every scientist to take part in this. Meet the Professor is a fantastic way to spark children’s interest in science.”
